Case Information: A 34-year-old male presented with nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite for 10 days. He reported a history of excessive thirst, frequent urination, nighttime urination, and recurrent carpopedal spasms during childhood. He was born at full term via normal vaginal delivery with no complications during the antenatal or neonatal periods. The patient denied any history of limb paralysis or weakness, recurrent urinary tract infections, fractures, hearing issues, or vision loss. There was no family history of renal diseases. Four years ago, his creatinine level was 2 mg%, and he was under the care of a nephrologist. Physical examination showed a moderately built and well-nourished individual with short stature (height: 140 cm) and no obvious deformities or skeletal dysmorphic features. Blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg, and both ECG and 2D Echo were normal. Laboratory tests indicated severe azotemia (urea: 139 mg%, creatinine: 10 mg%), hypokalemia (3.28 meq/L), hypocalcemia (5.0 mg%), and hyperphosphatemia (7.0 mg%) with normal sodium (140 meq/L) and chloride (96 meq/L) levels. Vitamin D levels were low (20 ng/ml) with normal PTH levels (90 pg/ml). Arterial blood gas analysis showed normal pH and low bicarbonate with respiratory compensation (pH = 7.41, serum bicarbonate = 18 mmol/l). A 24-hour urinary examination was limited due to decreased residual renal function with a urine output of approximately 100 ml/day. Immunological profile (ANA, dsDNA, Anti Sm, and Anti Ro/La) and viral markers (HIV, HbsAg, and HCV) were negative. X-ray of the lumbosacral spine and hands showed mild changes of renal osteodystrophy but were otherwise unremarkable. Ultrasound of the abdomen suggested medullary nephrocalcinosis with normal-sized kidneys, confirmed by a computed tomography scan. A percutaneous kidney biopsy from the lower pole of the left kidney revealed 1/6 glomeruli with segmental sclerosis, a large area of interstitial fibrosis, and diffuse dense infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells in the interstitium. Tubules showed intraluminal calcification and destruction, with unremarkable vessels. The patient was started on hemodialysis via a temporary right internal jugular venous catheter, and transplant evaluation was initiated.
Diagnostic Tests: The analysis revealed a homozygous missense variation in exon 2 of KCNJ1 gene in the chromosome 11 that results in the amino-acid substitution of glutamic acid for glycine at codon 167.

Case Information: A six-year-old male from a rural area presented with localized skin changes on the scalp, affecting the right parieto-frontal, left parieto-temporal, and occipital regions. The affected areas included three plaques measuring 8 × 6 cm, 5 × 6 cm, and 6 × 4 cm, respectively, with regular borders. The first two plaques had a red base, hair loss with hairs cut at the same level on the skin, pustules, and honey-colored and blood-stained crusts that fluctuated upon palpation and released purulent discharge. The third plaque showed diffuse hair loss and fine scaling on the surface. Additionally, there was bilateral cervical lymph node enlargement. The patient's mother reported the development of 'pustules' over the past two months, followed by hair loss. The patient had been treated with multiple topical azole medications without improvement. The patient had a history of Moebius syndrome, autism, and epilepsy, and was on risperidone for ongoing treatment. Imaging with the Fotofinder System GmbH® medicam 800HD (Columbia, MD) revealed erythema, black dots, comma hairs, broken hairs, interfollicular scaling, honey-colored crusts, pustules, and hair loss with hairs cut at the same level on the skin. Direct examination stained with chlorazol black was negative. Agar growth over four weeks on Mycosel® also yielded negative results.
Diagnostic Tests: A biopsy showed ulcerated skin, crusts, colonies of coccoid bacteria, an epidermis with parakeratosis, acanthosis with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, spongiosis, and exocytosis of lymphocytes and neutrophils. In the dermis, there was a diffuse interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils, lymphocytes, and histiocytes with foreign body multinucleated giant cells, bare stems, and fragments of squamous epithelium immersed in the infiltrate. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining revealed short spores and hyphae within and surrounding the hair shaft.

Case Information: An 11-year-old boy reported difficulty in eating and limited mouth opening for the past year. The patient described experiencing a burning sensation in the buccal mucosa when consuming spicy food during the same period. He had a habit of chewing tobacco and betel nut 15–20 times daily for the past 5 years and often kept the quid in the buccal vestibule. Clinical examination showed a maximum interincisal distance of 13 mm. Intraoral examination identified palpable fibrous bands over the labial and buccal mucosa, along with blanching of the palate, soft palate, and floor of the mouth. Tongue movements were restricted, and the uvula appeared shrunken.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathological examination showed moderately hyalinised collagen in connective tissue stroma. Few areas show thickened collagen bundles. Inflammatory exudate chiefly consists of lymphocytes and plasma cells.

Case Information: A 21-year-old woman was referred to the department of periodontology at the school of dentistry, Babol University of Medical Sciences for routine dental care. She was born to parents who were not related by blood, both of whom were clinically normal. Her mother was 22 years old and her father was 29 years old at the time of her birth. There were no pregnancy complications, and no other family members exhibited similar conditions. At birth, she presented with craniosynostosis, brachycephaly, and syndactyly of the hands and feet. The patient has mild mental retardation but demonstrates satisfactory social development and bonding skills. She has never had seizures. An extraoral examination showed a brachycephalic skull with midface hypoplasia, a flat forehead, depression of the temporal bones, proptosis, hypertelorism, a short nose with a bulbous tip and septal deviation, and a trapezoidal-shaped mouth. A lateral cephalogram indicated hypoplasia of the maxilla, giving the appearance of a class III skeletal relationship. Syndactylies were observed in the right hand’s third, fourth, and fifth digits and the left hand’s second, third, and fourth digits. Both feet exhibited fusion of all toes. Intraoral evaluation revealed poor oral hygiene with varying degrees of periodontal involvement, an arched swelling (pseudo cleft configuration), class III malocclusion, anterior open bite, posterior cross-bite, supernumerary teeth, ectopic eruption, and creamy white enamel opacities. The tongue appeared excessively large, and the maxillary arch was v-shaped.
Diagnostic Tests: The CT scan revealed palatal cleft and maxillary hypoplasia and nasal septum deviation.

Case Information: A 24-month-old Japanese boy was brought to our hospital for assessment of his short stature. He was born at 38 weeks and 4 days gestation with a submucous cleft palate and micrognathia. His birth weight was 3225 g (+0.53 SD for average Japanese male infants), and his birth length was 45 cm (−1.80 SD). The submucous cleft palate was surgically repaired at 18 months, and tympanostomy tubes were inserted for secretory otitis media. Auditory brainstem response testing was normal. At 22 months, bilateral leukocoria was observed, and phacoemulsification with anterior vitrectomy for bilateral lens opacities was performed at another hospital. He was noted to have Pierre Robin sequence, but the connection to his eye symptoms was not explored. He received speech therapy for speech delay. Upon presentation, his weight was 11.6 kg (−0.33 SD) and his height was 79.1 cm (−2.52 SD). His arm span measured 79 cm, and his sitting height was 48.5 cm (sitting height/height ratio 0.61). Physical examination revealed ocular hypertelorism, prominent eyes due to shallow orbits, a flat midface with a depressed nasal bridge, anteverted nares, micrognathia, low-set ears, and limited bilateral elbow flexion. There was no hypotonia, hyperextensible joints, or joint pain. His family, including his parents and two brothers, were healthy. His parents are not consanguineous. His father's height was 182 cm (+1.93 SD for average Japanese adult men), and his mother's height was 147 cm (−2.09 SD for average Japanese adult women). Radiographs indicated thickening of the calvaria, widening of the distal humeral metaphysis, absence of femoral head ossification, deformity of the femoral neck, and distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphyseal ossification centers, consistent with mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia. Serum insulin-like growth factor-1 was 20.17 nmol/L (154 ng/ml) (normal range 2.36–20.17 nmol/L [18–154 ng/ml]). An L-arginine stimulation test for growth hormone (0.5 g/kg arginine) showed a peak growth hormone level of 16.4 ng/ml. A luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone/thyrotropin-releasing hormone stimulation test (3 μg/kg luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone; 10 μg/kg thyrotropin-releasing hormone) showed prepubertal and normal thyroid-stimulating hormone responses. His karyotype was 46,XY. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed no abnormalities. Echocardiography revealed no mitral valve prolapse. No mutation was found in exons or exon/intron boundaries of the COL11A1 gene.
Diagnostic Tests: Sequence analysis showed a novel heterozygous mutation in exon 19 of COL2A1, c.1142G > A (p.Gly381Asp). The glycine at amino acid 381 was located in the Gly-X-Y triplet repeats region of the type II collagen triple helix, and it is phylogenetically conserved throughout species. This variant has not been described in the Single Nucleotide Polymorphism database, the 1000 Genomes Project, Leiden Open Variation Database 3.0, or the Human Genetic Variation Database in Japanese.

Case Information: A 79-year-old woman experienced a fall while ascending stairs, leading to a chest injury. A chest computed tomography scan identified a mass in the left breast. Further breast-specific imaging was conducted, and multiple core samples from the left breast were obtained. Two areas showed fibroadenoid changes and were consistent with each other. The patient has a family history of breast cancer in her daughter. Her medical history includes hypertension and morbid obesity. Her overall performance status was good.
Diagnostic Tests: A 1.5-cm, upper inner left breast mass was interpreted to be an invasive ductal carcinoma with basaloid features on core biopsy. This was estrogen receptor low positive (1%), progesterone receptor negative, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 negative.

Case Information: A one-year-old female presented with swelling in the right inguinal region. The family history included consanguinity, with the parents being first cousins. Physical examination identified bilateral palpable gonads located in the inguinal area. The external genitalia appeared female, with a slight clitoral enlargement measuring 1.5 cm, and separate vaginal and urethral openings. Ultrasonography did not reveal any Mullerian structures, and the gonads were situated in the inguinal canal. The karyotype analysis showed 46,XY.
Diagnostic Tests: The test results showed that there was impairment in testosterone biosynthesis. Testosterone/dihydrotestosterone ratio was 3.6. Testosterone/androstenedione ratio was found to be 0.107. Genetic analysis showed a homozygous mutation c.761_762delAG corresponding to p.E254VfsX10 in the patient; both parents were heterozygous.

Case Information: An 18-month-old female infant arrived at the emergency department following a brief episode associated with fever. She was born after an uneventful pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks gestation. Her motor and social developmental milestones were achieved within expected timelines, though she exhibited mild expressive speech delay, speaking only five to six words and unable to combine words at 18 months. Family history included a cousin with childhood-onset epilepsy and another cousin with febrile seizures. Upon arrival, the infant displayed lateralized eye gazing, unilateral facial twitching, and unilateral body shaking. She had a fever and upper respiratory symptoms but no signs of serious or central nervous system infection. Postictal examination was reassuring with no focal neurological signs. Extensive infectious workup returned negative results. During her hospital stay, she experienced two additional similar episodes. Due to the recurrence and specific onset characteristics, she was started on levetiracetam for a short-term course. An EEG study was normal. Brain MRI showed a borderline Chiari 1 malformation but was otherwise unremarkable, with no evidence of hippocampal sclerosis or focal cortical dysplasia.
Diagnostic Tests: Chromosome microarray revealed p.P54L heterozygous autosomal dominant pathogenic variant of GABRB3.

Case Information: A 36-year-old male, active smoker with no significant medical history and a family history of cancer in the mother (type unknown), presented with right-sided chest pain for 3 months, worsening over the past 3 weeks. Initially, he visited the emergency department 3 months ago when the pain began and was discharged after pain relief with ibuprofen. A chest x-ray (CXR) at that time was clear. On current presentation, vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds over the right lung; other findings were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed platelets at 729,000/µL, international normalized ratio of 1.46, prothrombin time of 16.5 seconds, partial thromboplastin time of 38.8 seconds, and D-dimer at 995 ng/mL. The CXR indicated a large right-sided pleural effusion. A computed tomography (CT) angiogram of the chest revealed multiple right-sided extra-pleural or pleural-based masses with a large right pleural effusion, masses eroding adjacent ribs, lateral margin of the T6 vertebral body, possibly involving the adjacent neural foramen, and partially extending through intercostal spaces. A significant portion of the mass was indenting the heart and displacing it to the left, with potential cardiac invasion. The patient underwent right-sided thoracentesis. Pleural fluid cytology indicated severe mixed acute and chronic inflammation with scattered uninucleate epithelioid-type histiocytic cells and an isolated large Langhans-type multinucleated histiocytic cell, suggestive of a granulomatous inflammatory process. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cervical/thoracic/lumbar spine and CT of the abdomen/pelvis were performed for staging. The MRI of the brain and cervical/lumbar spine were negative for metastases. The MRI of the thoracic spine showed a right paraspinal soft tissue mass with direct invasion of the right side of the T6 vertebral body. CT of the abdomen/pelvis with intravenous and oral contrast with liver protocol showed porta hepatis lymphadenopathy measuring 3.1 cm. No neurosurgical intervention was performed as there were no clinical or radiological signs of cord compression. An echocardiogram revealed a large posterior extracardiac mass compressing both atria with a small pericardial effusion, primarily along the right ventricular free wall, with diastolic invagination of the right ventricular free wall.
Diagnostic Tests: The pathology showed invasive poorly differentiated carcinoma and a high grade of uncertain histogenesis. Immunohistochemistry was positive for EPCAM (MOC 31), AE-1/AE-3, CAM5.2 (focally), DIM staining with p40 (negative CK5/6), synaptophysin, and CDX2 (focally) and negative for chromogranin A, CD56, CK7, CK20, TTF-1, NAPSIN A, GATA-3, S-100, SOX-10, and PAX8. Ki67 was 70%-80%, and the programmed death ligand (PDL)-1 tumor proportion score was 45%-50%.

Case Information: A 48-year-old woman, generally in good health, with occasional smoking habits and no family history of breast cancer, underwent a cosmetic bilateral mastopexy augmentation at age 28. She initially received 380 cc textured-surface implants placed in the sub-glandular plane. A year later, she opted for an implant exchange to 305 cc textured implants in the same plane, along with a re-mastopexy. Three years after that, she received 210 cc Allergan Biocell®-textured round TSM implants, again with a re-mastopexy. Ten years post-surgery, she experienced pain, swelling, and discomfort in her left breast without signs of infection or trauma. Ultrasound imaging of the left breast and fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of 50 cc serous fluid were performed, and the condition was deemed benign. Both implants and the surrounding inner capsule were removed, and a left breast outer capsulectomy was performed, with uneventful healing. No pathological review was conducted due to the absence of specimens. Six years later, she reported painful swelling in the upper left breast for three months, with no recent trauma, physical activity, or infection. Ultrasound identified a 9.5 cm sub-glandular fluid collection, and 100 cc of clear serous fluid was aspirated. Cytology indicated amorphous acellular material with no signs of malignancy. The seroma recurred three weeks after drainage. An intact seroma cavity was surgically removed with an en-bloc capsulectomy containing approximately 200 cc of serous fluid. The inner surface of the capsule showed a smooth luminal surface with fibrous tissue and fibrin cords, with no signs of free silicone or silicone granulomas.
Diagnostic Tests: The cytology report revealed the presence of large atypical cells positive for CD30 and CD3 and negative for ALK. The bacterial cultures from the serous fluid returned negative. The pathology report on the capsule described a fibrous tissue with a fibrinous covering, small-size lymphocytes, and clusters of large, atypical, invasive cells in the fibrous tissue. These cells exhibited positivity for CD30 and CD3 and negativity for ALK.

Case Information: A 3-year-old male child, born to consanguineous parents, presented with global developmental delay, hypotonia, lower limb tremors, and poor feeding. The child had a history of recurrent fever, cold, and cough since the age of 1 year. Over the past 6 months, the parents observed increased irritability. At 2 years old, the child was able to walk with support and speak monosyllables, but subsequently, there was a regression of these learned skills.
Diagnostic Tests: Brain MRI studies of the proband showed moderate confluent FLAIR/T2 hyperintense signal in the periventricular and deep white matter of bilateral frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes. In addition, FLAIR/T2 hyperintense signal was noted in corpus callosum involving genu and splenium. A mild FLAIR hyperintense signal was also noted in the bilateral deep cerebellar white matter. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood using salting out technique and was subjected to a targeted exome sequencing study. Variant filtration and prioritization analysis revealed a homozygous variant c.688T > G (p.Cys230Gly) in exon 6 of the PSAP gene (NM_002778.4). This variant has not been reported in the 1000 genomes and gnomAD databases. The in-silico prediction of the variant is damaging by SIFT, PolyPhen-2, PROVEAN, and MutationTaster. The variant was classified as likely pathogenic as per the ACMG-AMP guidelines and ClinGen framework with the following criteria—PP3 (strong) and PM2 (moderate).

Case Information: A 26-year-old woman reported a gradual decrease in vision over 5 months in her right eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a mild subepithelial haze on the cornea and a hammered metal appearance of the endothelium. The anterior chamber was shallow, and the iris pattern was disrupted with multiple dark brown nodules and ectropion uveae in the superior and temporal quadrants, leading to pupillary distortion. The fundus examination of the right eye showed advanced optic neuropathy with significant thinning of the neuroretinal rim and a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.9:1. The left eye appeared normal. Intraocular pressure (IOP) measurements were 40 mmHg in the right eye (treated with oral acetazolamide, topical timolol 0.5%, and brimonidine 0.15%) and 12 mmHg in the left eye. Gonioscopy indicated three quadrants of peripheral anterior synechiae in the right eye (covering the entire superior angle and inferonasal angle) and a normal angle in the left eye. Visual field testing showed advanced glaucomatous changes in the right eye with a mean deviation (MD) of -12.76 dB and pattern standard deviation (PSD) of 9.33 dB, with a probability (P) of less than 0.5%, while the left eye had a normal visual field.
Diagnostic Tests: Specular microscopy of the right eye showed pleomorphic endothelial cells with dark-light reversal typical of “ICE cells.”

Case Information: This 2-year-old girl is the second daughter of healthy parents with no known consanguinity. There is no family history of neurological or inherited diseases. She was delivered at term via cesarean section following an uneventful pregnancy. Her Apgar score was 9 at 5 minutes. Birth measurements were as follows: weight 3560 grams (50–75%), length 49.5 cm (25–50%), and head circumference 35 cm (50–75%). The neonatal period and early months of life were unremarkable. At approximately 7 months old, cyanosis was noted in her extremities and lips. Psychomotor delay was evident as she did not achieve head control or vocalization milestones. By 1 year of age, she exhibited alternating squints and abnormal head posturing. At 14 months, a neurological examination showed alternating squint, tetraparesis with appendicular spasticity and axial hypotonia, psychomotor delay with poor social eye contact, lack of vocalization, and incomplete head control. The Griffiths Developmental Scale indicated a mental age of 6 months. Brain MRI revealed a complex malformative condition with features partially resembling PCH. During sedation for the MRI, the patient experienced desaturation to 82–83%, with minimal improvement upon oxygen supplementation.
Diagnostic Tests: Blood gas analysis indicated a MetHb of 20%.

Case Information: A 24-year-old female presented with gingival enlargement. She was born as one of twin females after a full-term, uncomplicated pregnancy. Her parents, aged 32 and 34 at conception, are healthy nonconsanguineous Indian individuals. Clinical examination showed enlargement of the maxillary and mandibular gingiva, including the hard palate, partially or completely covering the crowns of maxillary posterior teeth. Multiple carious teeth were noted, along with prominent labial fullness on extraoral examination. Additional findings included mild mental retardation, hirsutism, large cartilaginous parts of the ears and nose, dysplastic fingernails, aplasia of nails on the last two toes of both feet, and pes cavus deformity. Preoperative radiographs indicated an abnormal position of maxillary posterior teeth. Examination of her twin sister, mother, and father showed no abnormalities. Radiographic examination of the foot revealed hypoplastic distal phalanges of the fourth and fifth toes. No abnormalities were found in cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, ophthalmologic, and blood examinations. The liver was normal in size, and the spleen was not palpable. Informed consent was obtained from all participants included in the case report.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathological examination of excised tissues revealed an acanthotic, nonkeratinized, stratified squamous epithelium, with elongated rete pegs. Beneath the epithelium, there were dense bundles of collagenous fibrous tissue.

Case Information: A 26-year-old right-handed male financial analyst presented with recurrent episodes of rotatory vertigo accompanied by nausea and palpitations. These episodes occurred three to four times daily without any specific time pattern. The initial episode lasted approximately 10 minutes, while subsequent episodes were shorter, lasting 10 to 15 seconds. The onset of these episodes was not associated with changes in head position. The symptoms had persisted for six months and did not respond to physical therapy or Lorazepam. An orthopedist ruled out a cervical origin by noting an almost natural curve of the cervical spine. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an irregularly shaped lesion in the right temporal lobe, measuring 2.0 × 2.4 cm. Electroencephalogram (EEG) results were negative. In our clinic, a consistent, spontaneous downbeat nystagmus (DBN) was observed, which intensified with head shaking and diminished in the supine position. Caloric test and audiometry results were unremarkable. During a follow-up visit, the patient experienced a brief episode with a déjà vu sensation. A 24-hour EEG monitoring recorded ictal sharp and slow waves originating from the temporal lobe, coinciding with the onset of vertigo and palpitations. Rhythmic changes lasting 15 to 20 seconds were also detected by synchronous EEG.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathologic analysis of the tumor demonstrated classical grade I findings: circumscribed neuroglial tissue composed of mature ganglion cells existing in a background of low-grade astrocyte-like cells with coarse processes. Ganglion cells contained Nissl substance and vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli and were randomly distributed in a haphazard fashion without polarization of cell processes. Molecular-genetic diagnosis included BRAF-V600E mutation.

Case Information: A 71-year-old male presented with abdominal distension and no other discomfort. Symptoms of bloating began a month prior and worsened in the week before admission. Two years ago, the patient had physical examinations and liver function tests at a local hospital and received liver protection treatment, but liver function did not improve. Occasionally, the patient experienced yellow urine but no significant physical discomfort. Personal and family history were unremarkable. Upon admission, vital signs were: body temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 68 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 134/74 mmHg, and blood oxygen saturation 99%. Physical examination revealed chronic liver disease, moderately yellowish skin and sclera, but no liver palms or spider angioma. The abdomen was soft, without tenderness or rebound pain. Liver area percussion was negative for pain, and the liver and spleen were not palpable below the ribs. Murphy's sign was negative. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities. Liver function tests showed albumin 23.9 g/L (normal 40-55 g/L), alanine aminotransferase 135 U/L (normal < 50 U/L), aspartate aminotransferase 127 U/L (normal < 40 U/L), γ-glutamine acyltranspeptidase 131 U/L (normal < 60 U/L), total bilirubin 49.3 μmol/L (normal < 24 μmol/L), and direct bilirubin 17.3 μmol/L (normal < 6.8 μmol/L). Blood tests showed hemoglobin 116 g/L (normal 160-175 g/L) and platelet count 75 × 10^9/L (normal 125-350 × 10^9/L). Coagulation tests showed prothrombin time 16.4 s (normal 9.8-13.2 s) and international normalized ratio 1.46 s (normal 0.85-1.20 s). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, neutrophil count, and hypersensitivity C-reactive protein were normal. Stool and urine routine tests were normal. Hepatobiliary enhanced magnetic resonance imaging revealed an unsmooth liver contour, imbalanced liver proportion, enlarged left lobe, reduced right lobe, non-uniform liver parenchymal signal, and multiple diffuse nodules. T1-weighted imaging showed isointensity, T2-weighted imaging showed low signal, OutPhase signal was not lower than InPhase, and no significant abnormalities were observed in the liver parenchyma after enhancement. The main portal vein's internal diameter was normal, and the intrahepatic bile duct was not significantly dilated. The spleen volume was increased with no significant signal abnormalities. The examination indicated liver cirrhosis, splenomegaly, and ascites. Tests for coxsackie virus antibody, Epstein-Barr virus antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, and cytomegalovirus-DNA were negative. The patient had no history of alcohol consumption or inappropriate drug use. Antinuclear antibody and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies tests were negative.
Diagnostic Tests: A heterozygous missense mutation (c.710A>G) in the 33998775 position of exon 5 of the AMACR gene was found, which occurred in the protein CoA-transferase family Ⅲ domain. The frequency of this site in the normal East Asian population is 0.0001.

Case Information: A 15-year-old female presented to an outpatient clinic with a 3-day history of fever, cough, and lethargy. She had no prior medical conditions. On physical examination, she had a fever of 38.3°C, mild tachypnea, good oxygen saturation, and stable hemodynamics. Breath sounds were reduced in the left lung, with crepitation noted at the base. Laboratory tests revealed slightly elevated septic parameters, with a total white cell count of 17.6 × 10^3/μL and a platelet count of 487 × 10^3/μL, prompting the initiation of oral antibiotics. Due to persistent symptoms, she was brought to the casualty department several days later for further evaluation. Chest radiography revealed homogenous opacification of nearly the entire left hemithorax, obscuring the left heart border, aortic knuckle, and left hemidiaphragm, with a contralateral shift of the mediastinum. The right lung field was clear of any focal lesions.
Diagnostic Tests: Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax revealed a large low-attenuation enhancing mass within the left thoracic cavity, measuring 11 × 13 × 16 cm. The mass was thought to originate from the left upper lobe, causing the collapse of the whole left lung. No intralesional hemorrhage or calcification was observed. Nonenhanced areas are seen within the mass, which likely represent necrosis. The mediastinum shifted to the right. The distal left main bronchus was narrowed, with tapering and occlusion of its segmental bronchi. The pulmonary trunk and left pulmonary artery were also narrowed but remained patent. There was no fat plane between the mass and pericardium, with evidence of pericardial and left pleural effusions. The chest wall was not affected. There was no evidence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy or liver lesions. The tissue biopsy measured 15 and 18 mm. Microscopic examination revealed tumor cells configured in hypocellular and hypercellular patterns with an area of necrosis. The hypercellular area displayed primitive cells with blastematous appearances. The shape ranged from spindled to ovoid, with focal pleomorphic to rhabdoid cells having intense eosinophilic cytoplasm. Subepithelial mesenchyme with the collection of stromal cells and overlying native ciliated columnar epithelium were observed. A focal immature chondroid element was identified. Immunohistochemistry of the stromal cells was strongly positive for vimentin and focal moderately positive for desmin. They were negative for EMA, pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), S100, smooth muscle actin, and myogenin. CD99 shows focal nonspecific positivity, while TTF-1 highlights the presence of native respiratory epithelium and alveolar pneumocytes.

Case Information: In March 2017, a 75-year-old male presented with a one-week history of left eye periorbital swelling, forward displacement of the eye, and swelling of the conjunctiva. CT imaging showed enlargement of the lacrimal gland and medial rectus muscle. Blood tests indicated macrocytic anemia, low white blood cell count, elevated C-reactive protein (44 mg/L), positive thyroglobulin antibody (404 U/L), and thyroid peroxidase antibody (108 U/L). IgG4 levels were elevated (2.5 g/L), while other immunologic tests were negative. Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM) showed diffuse thickening of the episcleral tissue. The patient was treated with prednisone 60 mg/day, leading to improvement and reduction of symptoms within 10 days. Over the following two years, he experienced three episodes of unilateral inflammatory orbital symptoms, requiring hospitalization. Prednisone was effective in two instances, while symptoms resolved without treatment in one instance. During the second episode, right eye posterior scleritis was confirmed by a typical T-sign on ultrasound. A lacrimal gland biopsy in December 2018 showed patchy lymphocytic infiltration with small T and B lymphocytes, and IgG4 staining was negative. Between 2018 and 2021, the patient had three additional hospitalizations for recurrent fevers, fatigue, weight loss, pulmonary ground glass opacities, and one episode of laryngitis. Blood tests during this period showed worsening pancytopenia and significantly elevated C-reactive protein levels (up to 236 mg/L).
Diagnostic Tests: Genome sequencing revealed a mutation in the splice acceptor site.

Case Information: The patient is a 9-year-old boy who was first seen at the neurology department at 6 years old. He had been previously admitted to the gastroenterology ward due to ongoing nausea and uncontrollable vomiting, with a notable weight loss of approximately 6 kg over the prior 2 months. Gastroenterological evaluations, including abdominal ultrasound, barium swallow test, and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, showed normal results. At 40 days old, he experienced non-febrile, infrequent multifocal motor seizures with fixed upward gaze and head movements, particularly during breastfeeding. Electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed frequent abnormal scattered epileptiform discharges, and phenobarbital was prescribed, resulting in seizure control. The medication was discontinued at 16 months, and he exhibited normal physical growth and neurological development until age six. He occasionally vomited once or twice a month without a clear cause, and proton pump inhibitors provided some improvement. He was born at 38 weeks gestation via an uneventful cesarean section to a nonconsanguineous family, with a birth weight of 3,050 g (z score = 0) and head circumference of 37.0 cm (z score = 2). He was admitted for prolonged physiologic jaundice in the first 2 weeks of life, with an indirect bilirubin level of 14 mg/dL, which resolved with phototherapy. His father and uncle had head circumferences above 2 standard deviations for their age but no clinical symptoms. At 6 years old, he experienced status epilepticus with generalized atonic seizures, followed by severe occasional projectile vomiting and recurrent daily nausea, particularly in the early morning and sometimes at midnight. Seizures were managed with sodium valproate and levetiracetam. He lost 6.0 kg (from 19.0 to 13.0 kg) over the next 2 months. At his first visit at this age, he had normal developmental milestones in speech, motor skills, and cognition. His weight was 13.0 kg (z score = -1) and head circumference was 52.5 cm (z score = 2). Ophthalmic examination showed normal gaze and pupil reaction to light. There was no palatal myoclonus, but nasal tone speech was noted. He had a weak gag reflex and significant drooling. Other cranial nerve examinations were normal. Knee deep tendon reflexes were exaggerated (3+), while others were normal (2+). Plantar reflexes were bilaterally downward. Gross motor function was rated 1 out of 5 (1/5) on the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) scale. Basic biochemical and metabolic tests, including thyroid and liver function tests, serum ammonia and lactate, urine organic acids profile, metabolic screen test (MS/MS), acylcarnitine profile, and serum amino acids chromatography (HPLC), were normal. A wrist X-ray was consistent with his chronological age.
Diagnostic Tests: The first MRI at the age of 6 years revealed faint bifrontal confluent deep and periventricular white matter signal changes, bilateral caudate nucleus involvement, significantly high in T2-W and low in T1-W images with garland and cystic changes around the tip of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles, especially the left side. In addition, a hyperintensity tumefactive lesion was identified in the brain stem area around the floor of the fourth ventricle and area postrema. No restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient map sequences were detected. Post-contrast T1-W images showed contrast enhancement in brain stem lesions. The repeated brain MRI at age of 8 years showed enlargement of the lesion in the area postrema extending to posterior pons and involvement of bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) detected a heterozygous mutation, c.262 C > T; R88C in the exon 1 of the Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP). Sanger sequencing confirmed that this mutation is de novo.

Case Information: A 28-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented with persistent skin nodules on the trunk and extremities. Symptoms began 4 years ago, accompanied by spiking fever, nausea, and vomiting. These initial symptoms resolved after 6 months but recurred with generalized weakness, joint pain, chest pain, and multiple firm, subcutaneous nodules. The nodules were non-tender, prone to ulceration, and self-resolving. Initial histopathology from an outside institution suggested a different condition, leading to azathioprine therapy despite negative lupus serology. Imaging studies at that time did not show any ongoing systemic issues. Although the fever improved, the nodules persisted and progressed after one year of treatment, prompting the initiation of methotrexate and oral prednisone. Clinical examination revealed erythematous and indurated subcutaneous nodules scattered on the arms and legs, as well as an erythematous and indurated plaque with central necrotic crust on the back.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathology of two different nodules demonstrated similar findings, revealing an epidermotropic, dermal and subcutaneous infiltrate comprised of medium-to-large, atypical lymphocytes and numerous histiocytes forming granulomas. There was notable angiodestruction, necrosis and syringotropism. Immunohistochemical stains showed the atypical lymphocytes to be positive for CD3, CD8, CD56 and TCR δ with loss of CD7 and diminished expression of CD5. These cells were negative for CD4, CD20, CD30, EBV in situ hybridization, CD34, CD117, MPO and TdT. Beta F1 was negative in the malignant cells while highlighted in the benign CD4 T-lymphocytes. The histiocytes appeared to be of non-Langerhans type and expressed CD63 (PGM1) and CD163. CD68/163 cells represented around 70% of the malignant infiltrate. The presence of granzyme and TIA confirmed the cytotoxic nature of the infiltrate. A T-cell gene rearrangement study was additionally performed and confirmed a clonal T-cell population.
